doc.title: Dan Wall and Adam Nussbaum interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 19, 2001

title: Nussbaum's milestones: Scofield, Liebman and Stan Getz
summary: Nussbaum names his first European tour with Scofield, the Liebman band in 1978, and playing with Stan Getz as validating experiences.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: Yeah. Is there a point that you can think back that was a good step up into the world of a professional musician, playing with some person or some band and that you felt like I finally got to point where I’ve been hoping for?
I know it’s hard to think back.
You mean a point where you felt validated?
Yeah I guess you could put it that way.
Well I guess maybe when you have one of your first big gigs, or maybe your first tour or something like that.
Well what was the first big gig for you?

Well the first band that I really worked in I played with, I did a tour with John Scofield in 1978 that was my first European tour, and that was a tour. And then I was working with Dave Liebman in ’78. And that was a very, very nurturing experience for me. I was the young blood and I was playing with Dave who’d played with all my heroes, you know, Elvin Jones, Miles Davis and that band also included a fantastic trumpet player from Japan, Terumasa Hino, John Scofield was in that band and eventually it was Ron McClure on bass. So these were all more experienced people than me. And to have that opportunity to play with them was really good and Dave is a great teacher. So for me to be in that situation night after night was very beneficial for me. And then I think having a chance to then work with Stan Getz, that validated me in another sense because a lot of people when they saw me with Dave, that band was a hard hitting band. And a lot of people didn’t like what we were doing, maybe we were stretching too much but it was really take no prisoners kind of situation. But then when you play with a master, like Stan, who is acknowledged across the board for his artistry, that validated me in another way. Because then people could see I just wasn’t playing with these guys going crazy all the time. We could play a nice bossa nova and things like that, and to play with somebody who played as great as he did was an amazingly great experience for me. You know this guy had an amazing sound, beautiful lines, incredible time, you know, he didn’t even know why he sounded as good as he did. He was that kind of natural musician. And that I think gave me another kind of a validation in other circles. But I just consider every experience that I have an opportunity to learn something else about this music. And I consider myself a work in progress.
